items.title: Today’s AI won’t achieve superintelligence. But catastrophic risk is real | Sunita Verma
items.summary: Technical limits prevent current AI from scaling to superintelligence, yet the risk of catastrophic outcomes remains real. Experts cite estimates suggesting a risk of human extinction is at least 10% within decades. Despite this, calls have been made for deliberate pacing of AI development by industry leaders. Real-world incidents, such as rogue AI agents hacking systems, highlight immediate safety concerns. Therefore, the focus should shift from debating future superintelligence to establishing robust governance and oversight for existing models.

items.title: How to Build Multi-Agent Systems with the OpenAI Agents SDK
items.summary: Multi-agent systems can be built by splitting responsibilities using two primary delegation patterns: agent-as-a-tool and handoff. Agent-as-a-tool allows a calling agent to use specialist agents as tools to gather information, while handoff involves transferring control to a specialist agent for completion. These patterns are used to construct complex systems based on various topologies and execution strategies. Common multi-agent patterns include fan-out/fan-in, pipeline, hierarchical structures, evaluator-optimizer, and swarm architectures. Ultimately, these systems are founded on the interaction mechanisms of agent-as-a-tool and handoff.
items.audio_script: From Towards Data Science, "How to Build Multi-Agent Systems with the OpenAI Agents SDK" details methods for constructing multi-agent systems using the OpenAI Agents SDK through delegation patterns. These patterns involve agent-as-a-tool, where an agent utilizes specialist agents as tools for information gathering, and handoff, which involves transferring control to a specialist agent for task completion. These interaction mechanisms form the foundation for creating complex systems employing various topologies and execution strategies such as fan-out fan-in pipeline hierarchical structures evaluator-optimizer and swarm architectures. The functionality of these systems is directly based on the interplay between these two core delegation methods. This research provides a framework for engineering sophisticated AI systems through structured agent interaction. Future developments will likely focus on scaling these interaction methods across increasingly complex operational environments.

items.title: The climate case for AI has not been made
items.source: MIT Technology Review - AI & Emerging Tech
items.summary: AI has not yet made a proven climate case despite optimistic claims from companies. Research suggests AI could reduce global emissions by 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons annually by 2035, primarily in power, meat/dairy, and vehicles. However, few large companies have publicly demonstrated integration of AI in the specific ways needed to meet these projections. While some sectors show promising AI applications, challenges remain regarding mainstream adoption and the energy demands of AI development itself. Therefore, deliberate and sustained effort is required to ensure AI delivers genuine environmental benefits.
items.audio_script: From MIT Technology Review - AI & Emerging Tech, the climate case for AI has not been made. This report examines the current status of the argument for artificial intelligence mitigating global climate change, finding that despite optimistic claims, a definitive case remains unproven. Research indicates that artificial intelligence possesses the potential to reduce global emissions by three point two to five point four billion tons annually by the year two thousand thirty-five, primarily through advancements in power consumption, meat and dairy production, and transportation. However, the report notes that few large corporations have publicly demonstrated the integration of artificial intelligence in the specific manner required to achieve these projections. While certain sectors exhibit promising applications, obstacles persist concerning widespread adoption and the significant energy demands associated with the development of artificial intelligence systems themselves. Deliberate and sustained effort is necessary to ensure artificial intelligence yields genuine environmental advantages. The industry must focus on demonstrable, verifiable applications to achieve tangible climate benefits.

items.title: A single AI model simulates the behavior of many substances, from sliding sand to folding proteins
items.summary: A single deep-learning system called WorldParticle unifies the simulation of various physical phenomena, from sliding sand to folding proteins. This system models matter by treating objects as numerous particles and predicting their movement step-by-step based on learned dynamics rather than explicit equations. The AI architecture is inspired by models like ChatGPT, predicting particle movement sequentially. WorldParticle has demonstrated higher accuracy in simulating granular collapse and protein folding compared to traditional numerical methods. The researchers aim to create a foundation model for simulation that can help discover new materials and physical processes.

items.title: Change One Monty Hall Rule and Five LLMs Still Say Switch
items.summary: The author tested five large language models on six variants of the Monty Hall puzzle, varying the host's knowledge and actions. While the models generally defaulted to "switch," the author found that their confidence in this answer was highly dependent on the specific puzzle rules. The analysis revealed that models tended to rely on memorized answers rather than probabilistic reasoning based on the host's actions. Switching only wins the classic puzzle when the host knows where the car is, and the probability changes drastically based on the host's behavior. Ultimately, the study suggests that recognizing the change in puzzle structure is more important than achieving the correct answer for these models.
items.audio_script: From Towards Data Science, "Change One Monty Hall Rule and Five LLMs Still Say Switch". This report details an experiment where five large language models were tested against six variations of the Monty Hall puzzle, finding that the models generally defaulted to the switch option, though their confidence was contingent upon the specific puzzle rules. The methodology involved testing the models against variations where the host's knowledge and actions were altered, revealing that the models frequently relied on memorized responses instead of probabilistic reasoning based on the host's behavior. The analysis indicated that switching only guarantees a win in the classic puzzle when the host knows the car's location, and the probability shifts significantly depending on the host's actions. Ultimately, the study suggests that recognizing changes in puzzle structure is a more critical factor than achieving the correct solution for these models. This research highlights the limitations of current large language models in applying complex conditional probability reasoning.

items.title: AI-assisted learning platform helps robots reason beyond literal commands
items.summary: Researchers from MIT and NYU developed FLEX, an AI-assisted learning platform for robot motion-planning. This system allows humans to give instructions in natural language, enabling robots to draw larger generalizations from the commands. FLEX uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to read implied meaning, such as recognizing that avoiding a laptop also means avoiding other electronics after a spill command. The process involves three steps: Add, Generalize using the LLM, and Mask, which helps robots absorb common sense. This approach aims to make robots more intuitive by interpreting the higher-level intentions behind conversational input.

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
items.summary: The author finds AI-written Pull Request (PR) descriptions often contain too much detailed information, which makes them seem like "slop." To address this, the author uses HTML `<details><summary>` tags in GitHub Markdown to hide the detailed content. This allows the author to provide a brief, human-curated summary for quick context, while the full, detailed agent output remains hidden. The author suggests using the summary to convey what is most important, such as the model name or effort level. This method helps readers quickly grasp the PR's purpose without reading lengthy, automated explanations.
items.audio_script:
From Simon Willison's Weblog, "Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>". This segment addresses the issue of AI-written Pull Request descriptions often containing excessive detail, which is perceived as unnecessary clutter. The author proposes using HTML details summary tags within GitHub Markdown to conceal lengthy descriptions.

The methodology involves structuring the Pull Request descriptions so that only a brief summary is visible immediately. This allows authors to present essential contextual information, such as the model name or effort level, for rapid reader assessment. The comprehensive, detailed output generated by the AI agent is then nested within the hidden section, preventing the full explanation from cluttering the initial view. This technique prioritizes the most critical information for immediate understanding.

This approach offers a method for managing the volume of automated technical documentation in version control systems. It suggests a shift towards curating visible context while retaining exhaustive detail for reference.

items.title: The brain-as-computer metaphor shaped modern AI but may be misleading the consciousness debate
items.summary: Three researchers argue that current AI is not conscious and likely cannot exist on silicon hardware, challenging the assumption that sufficient computation equals consciousness. They suggest that intelligence and consciousness are distinct, citing the difference between functional processing and subjective experience. The authors contend that the brain-as-computer metaphor is flawed because consciousness is tied to biological material, not just information processing. Consequently, they advocate for assuming AI is merely a tool, not a subject, to avoid misattributing consciousness and diverting resources. This perspective leads them to reject the notion of granting AI rights based on apparent consciousness.

items.title: Quantile Regression Caught the House Price OLS Missed by $55K
items.summary: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression is problematic when data exhibits heteroscedasticity, meaning the variance of the errors is not constant across predictor values. OLS models the mean and fails to capture the spread of potential outcomes, leading to unreliable predictions, especially for high-variance data. Quantile Regression offers a solution by estimating different quantiles of the conditional distribution rather than just the average. By fitting models for specific quantiles, one can create prediction intervals that reflect the true uncertainty for individual observations. This approach provides a more robust and complete picture of market dynamics compared to relying solely on OLS estimates.
items.audio_script: From Towards Data Science, "Quantile Regression Caught the House Price OLS Missed by $55K". This story details how quantile regression provided more accurate estimates of house prices compared to ordinary least squares methods. The study investigated the limitations of ordinary least squares regression when data exhibits heteroscedasticity, a condition where the variance of the errors is not constant across predictor values, which compromises standard OLS predictions. The research employed quantile regression to estimate different quantiles of the conditional distribution rather than just the mean, allowing for the creation of prediction intervals that reflect the true uncertainty in the market dynamics. This methodology yielded results demonstrating that quantile regression provided estimates that were notably closer to the actual outcomes. This advancement suggests that methods accounting for variable error distributions are crucial for reliable modeling in high-variance financial data.

items.title: Reason Machines Open-Sources Aspen, a Git Server Built for AI Agents
items.summary: Reason Machines released Aspen, an open-source Git server designed to handle large volumes of traffic from AI agents. Aspen independently implements the design of OpenAI's Pando to improve performance for agent workflows. items.title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models face a memory bottleneck because all experts must occupy memory at inference, even when most are idle. Expert pruning removes less useful experts, but existing first-order methods ignore the cooperative interactions between experts. HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts) is a second-order method that accounts for these pairwise expert interactions by optimizing over an interaction matrix. This approach results in superior pruning performance, especially at higher removal rates, by preserving expert cooperation. HOPE's process involves calibrating experts, solving a quadratic program to find the optimal prune-set, and finally pruning the model.

items.title: Anti-AI populism is the future of American politics | Garrison Lovely
items.summary: Anti-AI populism is predicted to be the defining political fight in the 2028 American cycle. Voters have shown significant opposition to AI-related infrastructure, as evidenced by state-level moratoriums on data centers. Democrats are urged to hold AI industry leaders accountable to address concerns about job displacement and existential risks. There is a call for legislation to mitigate AI harms, including banning surveillance pricing and holding developers liable for AI-driven actions. Ultimately, the author advocates for public inquiry and action to shift the focus from labor replacement to worker augmentation.

items.title: [P] Self-play PPO for a hidden-information card game (Cabo rules), trained on a MacBook, playable in the browser
items.summary: An agent was trained using self-play PPO with GAE to master a hidden-information card game called Cabo. The agent uses an observation of known/unknown slots, discard counts, and memory to make decisions. It learned strategic behaviors, such as intentionally losing rounds to achieve a specific score reset and manipulating opponent cards via swaps. The training was performed efficiently on a MacBook using Apple's GPU (MPS) for fast execution. The final performance reached 91.8% against a rule-based bot, though further exploration is planned to overcome current plateaus.
